procedural_history.impugned_order: The judgment and order dated March 14, 1966, of the Mysore High Court in Criminal Revision Petitions Nos. 120 and 123 of 1966, which cancelled the bail granted to the appellants and ordered their re-arrest and commitment to jail custody.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants were convicted by the Sessions Judge under ss. 147, 148, 323, 324 and 325 read with s. 149, Indian Penal Code. They appealed to the Mysore High Court, and were released on bail pending the appeal. The State then applied to the High Court under ss. 498(2) and 561A, Criminal Procedure Code, for cancellation of the bail, alleging that the appellants were misusing their liberty and committing acts of violence. The High Court allowed the State's applications and cancelled the bail.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's order cancelling their bail. The appellants argued that the High Court lacked the power to cancel the bail once it had been granted under s. 426, Criminal Procedure Code. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeals, holding that the High Court's inherent power under s. 561A, Cr. P.C., was attracted to the case because the allegations against the appellants prima facie indicated abuse of the process of the Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the inherent power under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to cancel bail that was granted to a convicted person under Section 426 of the Code, especially in the absence of an express provision for such cancellation.

facts: The appellants were convicted and subsequently released on bail by the High Court under Section 426 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) while their appeal was pending.
The State filed an application to cancel their bail, alleging that the appellants were misusing their liberty and committing acts of violence.
The High Court, exercising its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Cr.P.C., cancelled the bail.
law: Section 426 Cr.P.C. allows an appellate court to suspend a sentence and release a convicted person on bail.

Sections 497 and 498 Cr.P.C. contain express provisions allowing for the cancellation of bail for accused persons (pre-conviction), but there is no such express provision for convicted persons released under Section 426.
Section 561-A Cr.P.C. recognizes and preserves the inherent power of the High Court to make orders necessary to prevent abuse of the process of the court or to secure the ends of justice.
application: The Court addressed the argument that the absence of an express power to cancel bail under Section 426 was a deliberate omission by the legislature, which would preclude the use of inherent powers.
The Court rejected this argument, concluding that the omission was not deliberate but a "lacuna" due to "oversight or inadvertence."

It reasoned that if the High Court had no power to cancel bail, it would lead to "fantastic results" where a convicted appellant could commit further crimes, intimidate witnesses, or attempt to abscond without the court being able to intervene.
The Court determined that the allegations against the appellants, suggesting they were misusing their liberty, constituted a prima facie "abuse of the process of the Court."
This abuse of process directly attracts the High Court's inherent power under Section 561-A, which exists precisely to prevent such situations and to secure the ends of justice.
Therefore, the High Court was entitled to invoke its inherent power to cancel the bail granted under Section 426.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court has the inherent power under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to cancel bail that was granted to a convicted person under Section 426. This power can be exercised in a proper case to prevent an abuse of the process of the court or to otherwise secure the ends of justice.

issue.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Chapter XXXIX and Section 426 of the Criminal Procedure Code constitute a complete and exhaustive statement of the High Court's powers regarding bail, thereby excluding any inherent power to cancel bail.

facts: Appellants were convicted, and pending their appeal, the High Court suspended their sentences and released them on bail under Section 426 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr. P.C.).
The State later alleged that the appellants were misusing their liberty and committing acts of violence.
The High Court, exercising its inherent powers under Section 561-A of the Cr. P.C., cancelled the appellants' bail.
law: The appellants argued that the Cr. P.C. provides a complete and exhaustive statement of the High Court's powers regarding bail.

They pointed out that while specific provisions like Section 497(5) and 498(2) expressly grant courts the power to cancel bail in pre-conviction cases, Section 426 (post-conviction bail) contains no such express provision.
They contended that this omission was deliberate, meaning the legislature did not intend for the High Court to have the power to cancel bail granted under Section 426.
Section 561-A of the Cr. P.C. recognizes the inherent power of the High Court to make orders necessary to prevent abuse of the court's process or to secure the ends of justice.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument, finding that the omission of an express power to cancel bail in Section 426 was not deliberate but rather an "oversight or inadvertence" by the legislature.

The Court reasoned that accepting the appellants' view would lead to "fantastic results," where a convicted person on bail could commit further crimes, intimidate witnesses, or attempt to abscond, and the appellate court would be powerless to cancel their bail.
The Court held that since the Cr. P.C. had a "lacuna" (a gap) on this specific issue, the High Court was justified in invoking its inherent powers under Section 561-A.
It clarified that Section 561-A does not create new powers but recognizes the powers the court needs to function properly and prevent abuse of its process.
The Court concluded that the appellants' alleged misconduct constituted an abuse of the process of the court, which directly attracted the application of Section 561-A.

The Court also distinguished a precedent cited by the appellants (*Lala Jairam Das*), stating that it dealt with the power to *grant* bail in a different context, not the power to *cancel* it, and was therefore not applicable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code are not an exhaustive statement on bail and do not exclude the High Court's inherent power. The Court ruled that the High Court was entitled to use its inherent power under Section 561-A to cancel the bail granted under Section 426 in order to prevent an abuse of the court's process and secure the ends of justice.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court has the inherent power under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to cancel bail that was granted to a convicted person under Section 426 of the Code, especially in the absence of an express provision for such cancellation.
appellant_arguments: Once the High Court has granted bail under Section 426, it has no power to subsequently cancel that order and recommit the person to jail.
There is no express provision in the Criminal Procedure Code that grants an appellate court the power to cancel a bail order it has issued.
The legislature has specifically provided for the power to cancel bail in other sections (e.g., S. 497(5)), and its absence in this context implies that no such power was intended to be given.
respondent_arguments: The High Court possesses inherent power under Section 561-A to cancel bail.
This power is attracted when the appellants misuse their liberty by committing acts of violence, as this constitutes an abuse of the process of the Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the provisions of Chapter XXXIX and Section 426 of the Criminal Procedure Code constitute a complete and exhaustive statement of the High Court's powers regarding bail, thereby excluding any inherent power to cancel bail.
appellant_arguments: Relying on the decision in Lala Jairam Das v. King-Emperor, Chapter XXXIX of the Code, together with Section 426, is a complete and exhaustive statement of the High Court's powers to grant bail.
This exhaustive nature of the provisions excludes the existence of any additional inherent power in the High Court relating to the subject of bail.
respondent_arguments: The precedent of Lala Jairam Das v. King-Emperor is not applicable because it dealt with the High Court's power to grant bail to someone appealing to the Judicial Committee, not the power to cancel a bail it had already granted.
The question of whether inherent power could be used to cancel bail was not the issue in that case, making its ratio decidendi irrelevant to the current case.

cases.case_name: The Crnim Prosecutor, Madras v. Krishnan
cases.principle: The exercise of inherent power under s. 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to cancel bail was not inconsistent with the provisions of s. 498(1) of the Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court has the inherent power under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to cancel an order of bail that was granted to a convicted person under Section 426 of the Code, particularly when the Code lacks a specific provision for such a cancellation and the exercise of this power is necessary to prevent abuse of the court's process or to secure the ends of justice.
obiter: The inherent power of the High Court under Section 561-A can only be exercised for the three purposes mentioned in the section and cannot be invoked for matters covered by specific provisions of the Code or in a manner inconsistent with them.
Section 561-A does not confer new powers on the High Court but merely recognizes and preserves the inherent powers it previously possessed.

No legislative procedural enactment can provide for all possible cases, and it is an established principle that courts have inherent powers necessary for their existence and the proper discharge of their duties.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In a proper case, the High Court has inherent power under Section 561-A of the Criminal Procedure Code to cancel an order of suspension of sentence and grant of bail made under Section 426. This power exists because the omission of an express provision for cancellation is an inadvertent legislative oversight, and the court is not helpless when faced with an abuse of its process, such as a bailed appellant committing acts of violence.
legal_tests_applied: The inherent power under Section 561-A can be exercised for one of three purposes: to give effect to any order under the Code, to prevent abuse of the process of any Court, or to secure the ends of justice.

Inherent power cannot be invoked in respect of any matter covered by the specific provisions of the Code, nor can its exercise be inconsistent with any specific provisions. It can only come into operation if the matter is not covered by a specific provision.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's reliance on the precedent of Lala Jairam Das v. King-Emperor was misplaced, as that case dealt with the High Court's power to grant bail to a person appealing to the Judicial Committee, not the power to cancel a bail it had already granted. The ratio decidendi was therefore different and not applicable.

The argument that Chapter XXXIX and Section 426 form a complete and exhaustive code on bail, thereby excluding inherent powers, was rejected. The court held that no procedural enactment can provide for all possible cases, and courts must have inherent powers for the proper discharge of their duties.

The argument that the absence of an express power to cancel bail (unlike in S. 497(5)) implies a deliberate legislative choice was rejected. The court concluded that this omission was manifestly due to oversight or inadvertence, not intention.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that the allegations against the appellants, involving misuse of their liberty and committing acts of violence, prima facie constituted an abuse of the process of the Court.
Because the appellants' actions constituted an abuse of process, the conditions for invoking the High Court's inherent power under Section 561-A were met.

The court found that the specific issue of cancelling bail granted under Section 426 is not covered by any specific provision of the Code, thus making it permissible to invoke the inherent power of Section 561-A.

The court drew an analogy to the historical judicial consensus that, even before Section 498(2) was enacted to provide an express power of cancellation, courts used their inherent power under Section 561-A to cancel bail granted under Section 498(1).
policy_considerations: A ruling that the High Court has no power to cancel bail would lead to an absurd and dangerous situation where an appellant, after being released on bail, could threaten witnesses, intimidate counsel, attempt to abscond, or commit acts of violence, and the appellate court would be powerless to intervene. The court reasoned that such a situation could not have been in the contemplation of the legislature.

The court affirmed the established principle that courts must have inherent powers, apart from express provisions, as they are necessary for the courts' existence and for the proper discharge of the duties imposed upon them by law.
